stem: Set A has 5 elements and set B has 3 elements. All elements of B are also in A. How many elements does A ∪ B contain?

per_option_rationale.rationale: B is a subset of A, so A ∪ B = A, which has 5 elements.
Student adds |A| + |B| = 5 + 3 = 8, ignoring that the elements of B are already counted in A.
Student reports |B| = 3, confusing union with intersection when B is a subset of A.
Student computes |A| - |B| = 5 - 3 = 2, applying a difference formula instead of union.

explanation: Because B is a subset of A, every element of B is already in A. The union A ∪ B equals A, so it contains 5 elements.

explanation_sections.punchline: B is a subset of A, so A ∪ B = A exactly. The union adds nothing beyond A. The answer is |A| = 5.
explanation_sections.approach: State the property: if B is a subset of A, every element of B is already in A, so A ∪ B = A. Contrast the confusable case: the formula |A ∪ B| = |A| + |B| - |A ∩ B| is for when overlap is unknown. Here overlap is total (all of B is in A), so the formula reduces to |A| + |B| - |B| = |A|. No computation needed.
explanation_sections.lesson: When B is a subset of A, the union is just A. Adding 5 + 3 = 8 applies only when A and B share no elements at all.
explanation_sections.timing: About 20 seconds. Read "all elements of B are also in A" and write 5. Eliminate 8 first: that answer assumes zero overlap between A and B.
